objects.name: Solar Wind Composition collector
introductoryTalk: That foil was left in sunlight for 77 minutes and it is still the best sample we have.
It caught the Sun's own atmosphere out of the solar wind, and we took it home.

rounds.title: What the foil caught
questionOptionsForUser: How do you catch something with no container?
What is actually in the solar wind?
Why are noble gases the point?
answerForEachOption: You leave clean foil in the wind. Atoms implant in the top micrometre, and you read the foil.
Mostly protons and electrons, with helium, and traces of everything heavier down to the noble gases.
They are the fingerprint of the Sun's bulk composition, which you cannot sample any other way.
Very. The Moon has no atmosphere and no magnetic field, so nothing shields it and nothing contaminates it.

rounds.title: Reading it later
questionOptionsForUser: Why is that worth a sample return?
Did it say anything about the Sun?
answerForEachOption: Solar-wind noble gases in the Sun's own ratios, and a heavier component from an ancient solar wind.
It sets the baseline composition of the Solar System, so meteorites and our own air can be measured against it.
The Sun has run denser and slower in the past, recorded layer by layer in the foil.
Yes. Later instruments have far better sensitivity, so some of it is still unopened on purpose.

rounds.title: Deploying it
questionOptionsForUser: Why was it put out in the sun?
answerForEachOption: It was fetched and deployed in sunlight, at arm's length, with the sheet facing the Sun by its own shadow.
To keep suit outgas and dust off the collector. Almost every lunar deploy rule comes from that.
A bay-sized sheet unrolled from a cassette, under 7 kg, which is a real price in launch mass for foil.
Dust on the face, and one careless glove. Both are why the site was chosen by a human and not a camera.

rounds.title: What came after
questionOptionsForUser: What does a solar probe do instead?
answerForEachOption: Genesis collected solar wind at L1 and came back in 2004, after a parachute failure that cost most of it.
Parker flies into the wind itself and measures the fields and particles directly, close to the Sun.
The Sun's composition is the reference point for everything else, and we can touch the wind but not the Sun.
Isotopes of the volatile elements at precision the 1969 foil cannot give, from a longer exposure.

QA.location: Mare Tranquillitatis, 32 m north of the LM — a foil sheet facing the Sun

objects.name: Passive Seismic Experiment
introductoryTalk: That box listens to the Moon and has never been switched off by anyone who could reach it.
We set it on the surface, wired it to the lander, and left it running on one lunar day of sun.

rounds.title: What it listens for
questionOptionsForUser: Did it hear anything you did not want?
answerForEachOption: Moonquakes, yes, and they come from tides and from a crust that is shrinking as it cools.
Meteoroids. Small ones, all day, at 20 km/s. The record is mostly a rain of impacts.
Deep moonquakes, 700 to 1000 km down, driven by the Earth's tide. Nobody expected the interior to answer that far.
Thermal events. The box flexes as sunrise arrives, and the first readings were the instrument waking up.

rounds.title: Why the surface
questionOptionsForUser: Why not leave it on the ladder?
What does regolith do to a signal?
answerForEachOption: A seismometer needs mechanical contact. It sat on the regolith with its feet packed down by hand.
It is a dry fractured blanket, so the surface waves it records are slow, scattered and strange.
A solar panel and a battery sized for one lunar day, which is why the traverse had to come back.
A survey camera on the LM, and then a person walking, looking for level ground and a clear Sun.

rounds.title: What it taught us
questionOptionsForUser: Why does that matter to a mission now?
answerForEachOption: Small: a solid iron-rich inner core inside a fluid one, about a fifth of the radius. Seismics and ranging pinned it.
Barely. A handful of shallow events a year, big enough for the later Apollo stations to record well.
Landing near a fault is a safety question, and this is the only long record we own.
The Apollo 12 crew walked back to their own and re-pointed it. Three missions did that by hand.

rounds.title: Working by radio
questionOptionsForUser: How did it talk to Earth?
What happened when the LM left?
answerForEachOption: Through the LM's UHF link while we were on the surface, then through the relay left running behind it.
The ascent stage impact rang the whole network on purpose: a known explosion, a known mass, a known time.
It calibrated the Moon. One blast seen by every station, at a moment known to the second.
1977, when the network was closed for budget. The boxes are still there, dead and undisturbed.

QA.location: Mare Tranquillitatis, 63 m west of the LM — level ground, feet packed in

objects.name: Laser Ranging Retroreflector
introductoryTalk: That plate of fused silica is the most useful thing we left up here.
It has been in the sun since 1969 and nobody has touched it since.

rounds.title: What it is for
questionOptionsForUser: What does a mirror on the Moon do?
Does it measure anything but distance?
Who still shoots lasers at it?
answerForEachOption: Range. Observatories fire a laser at it and time the return; the round trip is 2.5 seconds at best.
Centimetres, over 384,000 km. It is the best-tested distance in solar system astronomy.
The orbit. The Moon recedes from us 3.8 cm a year, dragged outward by tides on Earth.
Several observatories, on scheduled nights, at the ephemeris of a 1969 object none of them has visited.

rounds.title: Why glass
questionOptionsForUser: Why does it come back so bright?
answerForEachOption: Metal would absorb sunlight and warp. Fused silica survives it and stays flat to a wavelength.
Corner cubes return light parallel to where it came from, so it shines back at its own laser.
Two from Apollo, plus three left by Soviet landers. Only some of them still give a usable return.
Micrometeorites darken it over millions of years. Long after that it will still be sitting there.

rounds.title: Handling it
questionOptionsForUser: Did you have to aim it?
What was the risk in deploying it?
Why is dust a problem out here?
answerForEachOption: No. It is passive, and wide-acceptance, which is the only reason it still works.
Kicking dust across the optical face. The crew deployed it at arm's length, back turned.
Nothing washes it away and nothing settles it. Levitated dust is the local weather.
Slightly, and the return dropped. Later crews photographed it and cleaned one with a glove.

rounds.title: What it proved
questionOptionsForUser: Is the equivalence principle in there?
Why do you care about that?
answerForEachOption: The orbit, the libration, and a hard number for the Earth-Moon distance that geodesy still uses.
The orbit behaves differently than the models, and the interior turned out to be partly molten.
Yes. The Sun pulls Earth and Moon, and ranging shows they fall together to one part in 10 to the 13.
It is the tightest test of gravity you can run without leaving the Solar System, and it needs no power.

QA.location: Mare Tranquillitatis, 0.674°N 23.473°E — 58 m east of the footpads

objects.name: Eagle, Lunar Module descent stage
introductoryTalk: Watch your step. That is the only footpad on the Moon nobody has ever flown again.
Sixty hours ago this was the only thing between two men and the vacuum.

rounds.title: What is this machine
questionOptionsForUser: Why does it look like a spider?
answerForEachOption: Eagle. A Lunar Module, two stages stacked. The descent stage you are standing on stays here permanently.
The ascent stage above carries two men back to orbit. Nobody ever flew the bottom half again.
There is no air, so there is no wing, no brake, no runway, no streamlining. Nothing aerodynamic survives here.
So it grows legs, lands on them, burns its own structure as fuel, and stands up on the top. Ugly is correct.
Nine metres tall, four and a half across the footpads, fifteen thousand kilograms.
Which on the Moon weighs what two and a half tonnes does on Earth. That is the only reason it flies.
Armstrong and Aldrin. Four hundred and five thousand people put them in it.
Collins stayed above in Columbia, alone, twelve minutes out of contact on every orbit.

rounds.title: Getting down
questionOptionsForUser: Why is it covered in grey dust?
answerForEachOption: Mostly by hand. The computer was flying toward a field of boulders the size of cars.
Armstrong took the control hand, overshot the crater and flew east until the ground said clear.
About twenty-five seconds of margin at touch-down.
Below that the procedure was an abort: the ascent engine fires either way and you never come back.
A 1202 and a 1201, computer overflow, from a rendezvous radar feeding it data nobody needed.
The fix was already written on the ground. They called it up and the computer kept flying.
No weather, so nothing washes away. It is pulverised glass and rock, ground fine for four billion years.
And it clings, electrostatically. It got inside the suits and smelled like spent gunpowder.

rounds.title: Living here
questionOptionsForUser: How do you sleep in that?
Why does walking here look like bouncing?
answerForEachOption: Roughly sixty hours on consumables. They spent twenty-one and a half, every minute scheduled.
Twenty-two seconds of that schedule was the whole margin between a sample return and a scrub.
Standing up, in a cabin with no seats. One on the engine cover, one curled in the equipment bay.
It is the worst bed ever designed and it still beat not sleeping before a moonwalk.
A personal spacecraft: 21 kilopascals of pure oxygen, a water-cooled undershirt, four hours of nothing else.
Try opening a jar with oven mitts on, underwater, wearing a fishbowl. That is the glove.
One sixth of Earth weight, so a step becomes a hop and the crew developed a lope.
Every tool needs two hands, because a stiff glove gives you no feel at the fingertips.

rounds.title: What stays
questionOptionsForUser: Is any of this still working?
What did you take with you?
answerForEachOption: The descent stage, a flag, and a reflector still used to range the Earth-Moon distance to the centimetre.
A seismometer, a solar wind collector, and a disc with messages from forty nations.
The reflector: observatories still range off it. The seismometer recorded until the budget closed it out.
Everything else is in vacuum, so it does not rust and nothing grows over it. It will outlast the buildings.
Twenty-one point seven kilograms of rock and soil, sealed before anyone opened it.
Sealed both ways, so nothing from here could get out either.
Grumman, on Long Island. Twelve thousand people who argued for two years over whether the legs should fold.
Their program manager's own verdict: the ugliest thing he had ever been proud of. It brought them home.

objects.name: Perseverance-class rover
introductoryTalk: That is the field party. It has driven this delta for years with nobody in it.
It will still be working when the last of us is a name on a plate over there.

rounds.title: Why Jezero
answerForEachOption: Because a river ran into it. Jezero is a delta: sediment sorted by water, in one place, 3.5 billion years ago.
Orbiters, for twenty years, reading minerals and slope. Then one human decision about which boulder field to risk.
Signs of life that survived. Not cells: chemistry and texture, where water left them lying around.
Layered sand and mud, carbonates, and igneous rock you can date. A geologist's whole day in two kilometres.

rounds.title: Living off a robot
questionOptionsForUser: What is the worst part of the job?
How long is a sol here?
answerForEachOption: It plans its own path over terrain it has seen, then stops and waits for us to review the day.
Dust on solar panels is the classic killer, so this one carries a nuclear battery and never has to care.
24 hours 39 minutes. The clocks run in sols and the number in the caption is what people read.
It has slipped and tipped. The escape was rehearsed on Earth against a mock-up of that exact wheel.

rounds.title: What it carries
answerForEachOption: Two pairs of eyes at human separation, so the stereo is genuinely stereoscopic, and a laser that zaps rock.
To read chemistry from 7 m away, which saves the arm, the drill and the tubes for the good targets.
Touch: grinding a rind off rock, caching a core, and taking the picture no orbiter can take.
Mass and time. A human does all of this faster, and the mass budget is why it is a robot.

rounds.title: What it leaves
answerForEachOption: In tubes on the ground, in a depot east of here. A second mission was supposed to come and get them.
Because one lander that drills, caches and returns was never affordable. So it is two missions and a promise.
They are tearing themselves on sharp regolith. Somebody had to learn that on a robot first.
It drives towards nothing, photographs nothing for anyone, and is the best-engineered instrument on the planet.

QA.location: Jezero Crater western rim, 18.4°N 77.5°E — an ancient river delta

objects.name: Ingenuity-class airfield
introductoryTalk: This flat patch of ground is an airfield, and there is a helicopter buried in it.
Ninety-two flights. The design life was five.

rounds.title: Flying on Mars
questionOptionsForUser: How do you fly where there is hardly any air?
What does one percent air cost?
answerForEachOption: Big blades, fast, light. The atmosphere is one percent of Earth's, so the disc is huge and it turns at 2400 rpm.
A helicopter the size of a biscuit tin, 1.8 kg, with one percent of an atmosphere to push on.
Because an aircraft sees the terrain a rover will commit to, and it decides the route before the wheels do.
No. It flies a stored route by itself and lands wherever the ground allowed it to.

rounds.title: The hard part
questionOptionsForUser: How did it survive the first winter?
answerForEachOption: Night. Minus ninety with no radioisotope heat, so it survives by design rather than by power.
It was driven onto a south-facing slope so the Sun would warm it, and the plan was rewritten for that.
Four legs and a body, on a rotorcraft, on a planet, with no maintenance and no fuel truck.
A blade, landing on rough ground, two years past anything anyone claimed for it.

rounds.title: What it changed
questionOptionsForUser: Would you send a bigger one?
answerForEachOption: It scouted drives, found a rock that stopped a traverse, and proved powered flight off Earth.
Reconnaissance for crewed landings, sample retrieval over terrain a rover cannot cross, and cliffs.
A helicopter that carries instruments is the obvious next machine, and it is already on a drawing board.
Overbuild the survival and underbuild the mission. The five-flight plan got ninety-two.

rounds.title: Standing on it
questionOptionsForUser: Can you see it from there?
answerForEachOption: Flat, clear of boulders, with a slope the Sun can work on. That is the entire site survey.
Over the ridge, still bolted to its backshell, exactly where the terminal descent put it.
Not today: a three kilometre round trip in a sol, and the delta is the other way.
No. Two worlds, one horizon, and a radio link to a machine that cannot look back.

QA.location: Jezero Crater, 18.5°N 77.4°E — a flat sand sheet with a south-facing edge

objects.name: Sample caching depot
introductoryTalk: Those tubes are the start of a return mission that has not launched yet.
Ten cores of rock and regolith, sealed, sitting on another planet.

rounds.title: What is in the tubes
questionOptionsForUser: What is the risk in leaving them?
answerForEachOption: Cores: 15 to 20 grams of rock and regolith, drilled, sealed and numbered in titanium tubes.
Because an Earth laboratory is a hundred times better than anything that can land there, and this is the shortcut.
When Jezero had water, for how long, and whether anything grew in it. Dating needs samples, not pictures.
Nobody can check the seals. A future mission finds tubes in dust with no way to know they are shut.

rounds.title: Why a depot
questionOptionsForUser: Why not land the return vehicle now?
answerForEachOption: Because a Mars sample return is three spacecraft, and it is the most expensive thing planetary science has attempted.
Insurance. They are dropped in a scatter so that one bad landing cannot lose the set.
Photographed from both ends, from orbit and from the ground, to be found by a machine that has never seen it.
Then they stay exactly as they are for a very long time. Out here only radiation and dust are active.

rounds.title: Getting them back
questionOptionsForUser: How do you launch off Mars?
Has anything like that been tried?
What is the hard part scientifically?
Why is that worth the money?
answerForEachOption: A small ascent vehicle built here, fuelled there, off a pad nobody has ever used.
No. Every gram that has left Mars left because an impact threw it, and a few landed on Earth.
Sealing and certifying. Bringing Mars to Earth means proving nothing alive came with it.
Because the instruments waiting in clean rooms are a thousand times better than anything that can land.

rounds.title: Standing in it
questionOptionsForUser: What would a human do first?
answerForEachOption: An ancient lake floor: fine sand over cemented pebbles, and carbonate where the water did the sorting.
About 3.5 billion years, and it is the best evidence there has ever been for warm wet Mars.
Igneous ones you can date and sedimentary ones that hold the chemistry, both within a kilometre.
Turn over a rock nobody has turned over, look underneath it, then go find shade for the suit.

QA.location: Jezero Crater, ten sealed tubes scattered on flat ground east of the airfield

objects.name: Ares habitat and ascent vehicle
introductoryTalk: Captain. Easy, that dark ring is your own bootprint.
Everything under your boots is iron oxide. It is the only colour this planet has.

rounds.title: Getting down
questionOptionsForUser: How did you land this time?
Why is the descent so long?
What did you see out of the window?
answerForEachOption: The Moon was flown by hand. Mars is flown by a machine you cannot argue with for seven minutes.
Aeroshell, a supersonic parachute, then a skycrane that lowers you on a cable and flies off to crash itself.
There is an atmosphere, which is a brake and a threat at once: five kilometres a second of heat, 400 seconds of wind.
On the Moon there was nothing to fly through, so the whole landing was rocket fuel from orbit down.
Nothing, on the way in. Four minutes of plasma blackout, instruments only.
Then the ground appeared already close, which is the part every test pilot complains about.
Fuel, plenty compared with the Moon. Time was the margin here: no window opens twice a month.
Miss the date and the return is 26 months away, so an abort was never actually an option.

rounds.title: The wrong sky
questionOptionsForUser: Why is the sky the wrong colour?
answerForEachOption: Fine dust in suspension, all day. It scatters the blue out of the light and leaves butterscotch.
And it runs backwards at sunset: the same dust piles blue into a halo round the Sun.
Minus sixty on average, and it swings 60 kelvin in one day because there is hardly any air to hold heat.
Your suit is a thermos in that, and the habitat is a house that is also a pressure vessel.
Dust storms, seasonally: from whirls you photograph to events that wrap the planet for months.
There is no lightning. There is not enough air, and no water, to make it.
You are 1.52 astronomical units out, so the light is 43 percent of what it was at Earth.
The disc is a third across, and the panels are sized for that number rather than for the one you remember.

rounds.title: Twice the weight
questionOptionsForUser: Is walking harder than on the Moon?
What does the air do for you?
answerForEachOption: Thirty-eight percent of Earth against the Moon's sixteen. The hop is gone, you walk like a person again.
Same suit, so every movement you trained for is wrong. The lope that worked out there looks ridiculous here.
Yes, and that is the good news: a 100 kg tool is a 38 kg tool, which is why the site work is human at all.
What gravity gives back, the dust takes straight away.
Almost nothing for pressure, and everything for heat: you can shed waste heat into it, which the Moon never let us do.
It is also why the samples do not have to be protected from the outside, only from us.
Twenty-four hours thirty-nine minutes, so the crew keep Earth hours and call the count sols.
Two of the three watch systems in that habitat exist to put a shift in daylight.

rounds.title: Who else is here
questionOptionsForUser: Who else is out here with us?
What does the crew do first?
What do you fear out here?
Why is there a flag here?
answerForEachOption: Robots. One has driven this rim for years, longer than anyone has been off Earth.
It will still be working when the last of us is a name here, and that is the design requirement, not a joke.
Look up. Then pressure, then dust, then samples, in that order, every sol.
A human geologist does in a week what the rover managed in a year.
The suit, the dust and the return date, in that order, and not the cold.
Every loss in this business has come from something that was supposed to be routine.
Because the one over there took 400,000 people to plant, and the sunlight bleached it white.
It marks the site for whoever comes next, and it will outlast the building we arrived in.

objects.name: Sun-Earth L2 observatory
introductoryTalk: Take your time with the handholds. That mirror has been cold for years and it is still looking.
There is nobody out here. That is the entire point of the place.

rounds.title: Why L2
questionOptionsForUser: Why come all the way out here?
Is it a place you can park?
What is on the cold side?
answerForEachOption: Because L2 is the one direction where the Sun, Earth and Moon are all behind you, and you can radiate away from all three.
No. L2 is unstable, so it rides a halo orbit around nothing and station-keeps about once a month.
It is the design: one sunshield the size of a tennis court, permanently between the Sun and the cold side.
Forty kelvin of telescopes and detectors, in the shade, pointed away from the brightest thing nearby.

rounds.title: Floating out here
questionOptionsForUser: What is it like, being out here?
Can you go for a walk?
What does a spacesuit do here?
How long is an EVA out here?
answerForEachOption: Quiet. The Sun is always behind you, so your own shadow is permanently in front of your feet.
There is nothing to walk on. You are on a tether, in a suit, working off handholds on a machine.
Not enough. With no air to cool against, a suit in sunlight here is a survival problem, not a workspace.
On the station, six to eight hours. A repair like this one was planned as seven sorties and took weeks.

rounds.title: What it sees
questionOptionsForUser: Why not build bigger on Earth?
answerForEachOption: Everything faint and everything old: the first galaxies, and the air of planets around other stars.
Because expansion stretches early light into wavelengths the ground cannot see at all.
Because the atmosphere glows in the infrared and it twinkles. Both are fixed by going 1.5 million km away.
Nothing, and that is the surprise. The mirror came into focus better than the ground tests predicted.

rounds.title: Living there
questionOptionsForUser: Where does it go when it dies?
answerForEachOption: Until the propellant runs out, which was sized for ten years and bought by launch vehicle margin.
Micrometeoroids on the shield, and one part in a service module nobody can reach.
Nowhere. It cannot be deorbited from L2, so it is pushed into a disposal orbit that never returns.
Once. On a tether, in a suit, with no way down and a two week light delay on every answer.

QA.location: Sun-Earth L2, 1.5 million km from Earth away from the Sun — halo orbit

objects.name: Inner heliocentric solar probe
introductoryTalk: Look at the heat shield, then at the Sun. Only one of those two is designed to be there.
This is the closest anything has come to a star, and it is unmanned on purpose.

rounds.title: Flying into a star
questionOptionsForUser: How do you get that close to the Sun?
What is the temperature out there?
answerForEachOption: You do not fall in, you give up speed: seven Venus passes to shed the Earth's 30 km/s of orbital motion.
Fourteen hundred degrees on the shield face. Behind it the instruments sit near room temperature.
That is the mission. The surface is 5500 and the air above it is a million degrees, and nobody knows why.
Twelve centimetres of carbon composite, with the instruments behind it in a shade that never moves.

rounds.title: What it samples
questionOptionsForUser: What can you measure that Earth cannot?
answerForEachOption: The solar wind itself, every 88 days, in the region where the wind is still being made.
Fields and particles at the same instant, in the plasma, instead of 150 million km downstream.
Magnetic switchbacks, zig-zags in the field that turn out to start at structures on the surface.
It touches what comes off it. Nothing solid survives the corona and nothing solid needs to.

rounds.title: Surviving it
questionOptionsForUser: What is the hardest engineering problem?
What happens if a thruster fails?
answerForEachOption: Autonomy. The Sun blocks the radio path, so a lost link means a lost craft before anyone down here notices.
Six small thrusters and a star tracker asked to work 40 degrees from the brightest object in the sky.
The two that matter have redundancy, and there is a propellant budget that quietly decides the end.
Fifteen times what a panel gets at Earth, which is why the arrays retract into the shield's shadow.

rounds.title: Standing where you are
questionOptionsForUser: What does the Sun look like here?
How do you float out here?
answerForEachOption: A human needs a hundred tonnes of radiator to last ten minutes. This needs a shield and a battery.
Fourteen times the disc you left behind, and the sky is still black, because there is no air to light up.
You do not. You watch from a distance that keeps the numbers honest, through instruments built for this.
The same shield, bigger, with a sampler that brings coronal material home.

QA.location: 0.05 AU perihelion, inside Mercury's orbit — inside the solar corona
